# Golden files

These files are the gate in `docs/plans/HARNESS-PORTABILITY-PLAN.md` section 8.
A change to the importer or the reconciler merges only when its output matches
the golden, or the difference is an intended fix that ships its own test.

| File | Written by | Checked by |
|------|------------|------------|
| `importer-state.golden` | `SyncHarnessStats` on `testdata/memory`, dumped table by table | `internal/importer/golden_test.go`, `TestGoldenImportState` |
| `reconcile-dry-run.golden` | `scripts/reconcile-memory.py --dry-run` against a fake service | `scripts/test_reconcile_golden.py`, `ReconcileDryRunGolden` |

## Fixture cases

The shipped fixture carries the inputs for the reconciler's mission-ID and
step-status paths. Each is written in the Markdown shape Bishop writes. The
files are the source; this section does not list them.

- `findings/FINDINGS.md`: each fixture entry has a `**Mission**` field. Its
  Rationale says what the entry exercises.
- `state/MISSION-ARCHIVE.md`: the rows are the known mission ids the
  `**Mission**` fields are checked against. An id with no row here, and no
  folder under `missions/`, is not known.
- `missions/mission-20260904-01/PROGRESS.md`: a step row carries a status
  outside the step set.

Only existing files carry these cases. No file was added, because the
importer test asserts the exact document count. The importer golden embeds the
body of `findings/FINDINGS.md`, so an edit to that file changes it.

## Regenerating a golden

An intended change is recorded with update mode:

    UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 go test ./internal/importer -run TestGoldenImportState -count=1
    UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 python3 scripts/test_reconcile_golden.py

Update mode writes the file and then fails the test on purpose. Run the same
command again without `UPDATE_GOLDEN` to confirm. CI sets `UPDATE_GOLDEN` to the
empty string, so update mode never runs in CI. The tests fail on any mismatch
against the committed golden.

## What the goldens cannot see

- **Request payloads.** The reconciler golden records the method and path of
  each request the fake receives, not the body. A write's payload is not
  compared.
- **Nested mission files.** The fixture's mission folder holds flat files.
  A golden cannot kill a mutant that only changes behaviour for a deeper path.
- **Values the goldens do not read.** The goldens do not pin: `AgentsDir`
  (`internal/profile/profile.go:51`, read by `AgentsDirFor` in
  `internal/importer/agents.go:19`, which the Go golden does not call), the
  approver default `APPROVER_DEFAULT` in `scripts/reconcile-memory.py:102`
  (used at `:1146`), `DefaultHarness` (`internal/profile/profile.go:61`, read
  by `cmd/mcpd/main.go:98`), and `ReviewerRole` (`internal/profile/profile.go:60`,
  read by `internal/api/crew.go:206` and `internal/api/hud.go:193`). These are
  not on the paths the golden tests exercise, as read from their call
  sites. `APPROVER_DEFAULT` is now pinned by `ApproverDefaultTests` in
  `scripts/test_reconcile_units.py` and is mutation-tested below. `AgentsDir`,
  `DefaultHarness` and `ReviewerRole` are not, and are still unpinned.
- **Finding links and step status values.** The dry-run labels a finding by
  its date and target, and a step by its number, so a wrong `**Mission**` link
  does not appear in the golden. A finding or step that is warned appears as a
  WARN line on stderr and in the summary's "warned" count, so a warning that
  stops firing is visible; the value a step status was rejected for is in the
  WARN line. A dropped step row does appear, because its line is gone. The
  links are pinned by `FindingMissionLinkTests` and `FindingWarningTests`, and
  the step statuses by `StepStatusTests` and `StepWarningTests`, all in
  `scripts/test_reconcile_units.py`, which read the shipped fixture.
- **Journal paging.** The golden's fake never pages: it answers each
  flight-recorder GET with an empty array and no `has_more`, so the golden
  reads only the path a server that does not page takes. The paging path
  (`fetch_journal` in `scripts/reconcile-memory.py`) is pinned by
  `PagedJournalTests` and `PagedJournalExitTests` in
  `scripts/test_reconcile_units.py`, and the server's `offset` and `has_more`
  by `TestListFlightRecorderPaging` in `internal/api/flight_recorder_list_test.go`.

## Mutant record (DIR-017)

Each mutant is planted alone, its killers are run, and the file is restored and
checked byte for byte. The table below is generated from
[`mutants.json`](mutants.json), which is the single source. Edit the spec, then
run `python3 -I scripts/check_mutants.py --write-readme`. Do not edit the table.

`make test` runs the record check (`scripts/check_mutants.py`), which prints a
message for each error it finds. Failure text is not stored here. `make mutate`
(see Mutation testing below) produces it from a run.

### Guard mutants: not recorded, and why

The rule for the tests in `scripts/test_triage_run.py`: an invariant a test pins has a row above with its mirror, or an entry here with the reason it has none. This sweep, run from the repository root, prints every test that is no row's killer. Each name it prints is named in an entry below, and a name it prints that is not named below is a gap in this record.

    import json, re
    spec = json.load(open("testdata/mutants.json"))["mutants"]
    killers = {k for m in spec if m["status"] == "active" and m.get("suite") == "scripts/test_triage_run.py" for k in m["killers"]}
    cls = None
    for line in open("scripts/test_triage_run.py", encoding="utf8"):
        c = re.match(r"class (\w+)\(", line)
        cls = c.group(1) if c else cls
        t = re.match(r"    def (test_\w+)\(", line)
        if t and "%s.%s" % (cls, t.group(1)) not in killers:
            print("%s.%s" % (cls, t.group(1)))

Entries for those names, and for invariants a row does not pin on its own:

- **Last covering rule (`covering[-1]` read as `covering[0]`).** Not recorded. The grader's listing has two covering rules, an allow at rule 0 and the deny at rule 4, so the wrong choice fails the accept test and the refusal test for the last covering rule. Both were reported as run by hand against a scratch copy in an earlier round; they were not re-run for this record. The choice has no distinct opposite edge to pair with, so it has no row. The expression is `covering[-1]` in `scripts/triage-run.sh`; find it by that text, since a line number moves with every edit above it.
- **A refusal mapped to exit 4 (the 2-to-4 mutant).** Not recorded. Its opposite edge is GUARD-PY-REFUSE, which is already paired with GUARD-PY-ACCEPT. Recording it would re-pair an existing row, which this record does not do. The edit is the `return EXIT_REFUSED` under `except Refused` in the guard's entry point in `scripts/triage-run.sh`, changed to return `EXIT_CANNOT_CHECK`; find it by that text, not by a line number.
- **The positive control read one rule early (`range(last - 1, ...)`).** Not recorded. The two tests `GuardPositiveControl.test_guard_accepts_an_edit_allow_directly_before_the_final_deny` and `GuardPositiveControl.test_guard_accepts_an_edit_allow_that_a_later_deny_overrides` are the controls that would catch it, and no row names them. The first-rule pair is GUARD-FIRST-SKIP and GUARD-FIRST-DENY-REFUSE; the early read has no unused partner.
- **Permission-block parse shapes with no row**: `test_guard_accepts_a_definition_with_single_quoted_keys_and_values`, `test_guard_cannot_check_an_unmatched_quote_in_a_rule`, `test_guard_cannot_check_a_tab_indented_rule_in_the_permission_block`, `test_guard_cannot_check_an_odd_indent_in_the_permission_block`, `test_guard_cannot_check_a_nested_permission_line_with_no_value` and `test_guard_cannot_check_a_nested_permission_line_with_no_action`. The reason is that the edit each would need is the removal of one `raise CannotCheck("... cannot read permission line ...")` (the `raise CannotCheck` calls in `scripts/triage-run.sh` that carry that message) or of the pattern that feeds it, and the opposite edge of that is a shape read as a rule, which GUARD-NEST-DROP and GUARD-COMMENT-INDENT already pair elsewhere. A row would re-pair them. Their docstrings state the path they take and claim no kill.
- **`GuardCannotCheck.test_guard_cannot_check_when_opencode_debug_fails`.** Not recorded on its own: `GuardCannotCheck.test_guard_cannot_check_when_opencode_debug_fails_even_with_a_listing` is the killer of GUARD-DEBUG-ACCEPT, and this test differs only in printing no listing. It adds no edge.
- **`RunReportsErrors.test_run_error_event_message_reaches_the_log` and `RunReportsErrors.test_run_nonzero_exit_points_at_the_result_file`.** Not recorded, and there is no better reason than that: they test how `run_agent` reports a failed run (the error event, the non-zero exit), not the guard, they came with the OpenCode port (cdd0ad8), and no mutant was planted against them in this change. This is a gap in the record, named so that it is not read as covered.
- **The layered config's contents.** `LayeredConfig.test_run_declares_bishop_triage_as_a_v2_server_outside_code_mode` parses the config the script hands OpenCode, for each kind, and asserts the shape of `mcp`, `codemode`, the absence of `enabled` and of `disabled: true`, the command, and the profile and URL environment values; each of those has a row pair (the GUARD-MCP rows). A config value no test asserts has no row; for example the server's `type`, the `BISHOP_HARNESS` value, and the keys outside `mcp`. `LayeredConfigRealOpenCode.test_real_opencode_keeps_codemode_off_in_the_config_the_run_builds` also gives the grade run's config to the real `opencode api --standalone GET /api/config` (no model, no session, `HOME` in a temporary directory) and checks the server each listed document carries. It is a killer of GUARD-MCP-LEGACY-SHAPE, GUARD-MCP-CODEMODE-DROP and GUARD-MCP-CODEMODE-TRUE. With no opencode on the host it is skipped as "could not check", so there the parse test alone is the kill.
- **What the `enabled` and `disabled` assertions rest on.** One observation on OpenCode 2.0.32, pinned by `LayeredConfigRealOpenCode.test_real_opencode_lists_disabled_and_drops_enabled`: given a server with `enabled` false and `disabled` true, the listing carries `disabled` and no `enabled`. What a live session does with `disabled` was not observed. That test has no row, because nothing of ours decides what the binary lists; it fails only if a later OpenCode lists something else. GUARD-MCP-ENABLED-KEY and GUARD-MCP-DISABLED-TRUE keep a dead key and a disabled flag out of the config, and their properties say the same.
- **The config probe's classification.** `scripts/opencode_config_probe.py` runs that command and classifies the answer as checked, could-not-check or failed. Could-not-check, which skips the test, is: no binary, a binary that cannot be started, no answer in time, output that is not JSON, and a non-zero exit that a run on an empty config shares. Failed is: a non-zero exit the empty-config run does not share (the binary ran and refused the layered config, with its stderr in the reason), and exit 0 with valid JSON that lists no document carrying the grader's step cap (the binary ran and did not carry the config). `ConfigProbeClassification` drives every branch with a stub binary, and each GUARD-OCPROBE row pairs one edge of the classification with its opposite. Not observed: a real 2.0.32 exiting non-zero on a config. The two configs tried by hand that it did not carry, a string `steps` and a truncated JSON document, both exited 0 and listed no matching document, so the non-zero branch is exercised by the stub alone, and `LayeredConfigRealOpenCode.test_real_opencode_that_drops_the_config_is_a_failure_and_not_a_skip` is the real-binary instance of the exit-0 branch (the truncated document is not pinned).
- **The run flags.** GUARD-RUN-STANDALONE-OFF and GUARD-RUN-PURE-ADD pin the flag assertions of `GuardAccepts.test_run_is_started_standalone_without_pure`.
- **Pairs that are not opposite edges.** Each is two faults in one area, and the property of each row says what it removes. GUARD-DEF-OS-OFF (the error branch removed) and GUARD-READ-ASCII (the decode changed) are both on the definition read. GUARD-STRIP-BASH (tr replaced by a slow substitution) and GUARD-STRIP-NONE (no stripping) are both on the emptiness check of the listing. GUARD-DEF-UTF8-OFF (the decode error clause removed) and GUARD-DEF-UTF8-LAX (bad bytes replaced) are both on a definition that is not UTF-8; the opposite edge of both, a valid non-ASCII definition read as UTF-8, is GUARD-READ-ASCII, which is already paired. GUARD-COVER-OR (a rule covers by either star) and GUARD-COVER-DENY-ONLY (only a deny covers) widen the covering rule by shape and narrow it by effect. The GUARD-PREC rows are the ends of the order flag, then environment, then file: GUARD-PREC-FILE-OVER-FLAG and GUARD-PREC-FILE-IGNORED, GUARD-PREC-FILE-OVER-ENV and GUARD-PREC-ENV-OVER-FLAG. GUARD-HELP-SOURCES-ENV (help sources the env file) and GUARD-HELP-LOG-DIR (help creates the log directory) are both help with a side effect, as are GUARD-HELP-DEBUG-CALL and GUARD-HELP-RUN-CALL (help calls the stub for `debug`, or for `run`): two faults on one side. The opposite edge of each is the positive control inside the same test, a run that is not help doing that thing. The position pair (GUARD-HELP-FIRST-TWO and GUARD-HELP-SKIP-FIRST) and the arm pair (GUARD-HELP-H-OFF and GUARD-HELP-LONG-OFF) are opposite edges. GUARD-OCPROBE-TIMEOUT-REFUSED and GUARD-OCPROBE-UNSTARTABLE-REFUSED (no answer, and no start, read as a refusal) are two faults on one side, and so are GUARD-OCPROBE-STDERR-OFF and GUARD-OCPROBE-CONTROL-STDERR-OFF (the stderr left out of one reason, or of the other); each pair dies in different tests or cases.
- **The timeout pair.** GUARD-TIMEOUT-OFF removes the bound and GUARD-TIMEOUT-CODE changes the status the reason is keyed on. Both act on the timeout path: two faults on one side, not opposite edges. They stay paired as recorded, and their properties say what each removes. The bound's opposite edges are GUARD-TIMEOUT-SHORT and GUARD-TIMEOUT-LONG.
- **Kills by the run's time limit.** In the final run, GUARD-STRIP-BASH, GUARD-TIMEOUT-LONG, GUARD-TIMEOUT-OFF and GUARD-RETRY-UNBOUNDED fail with `triage-run.sh did not finish within 30 seconds; the run was killed`, which is `run_script`'s limit and not an assertion about time. The 10-second bound in the live-size test is a backstop that these mutants do not reach.
- **GUARD-STRIP-BASH depends on the host's bash.** The kill rests on `/bin/bash` being slow on a pattern substitution. On the bash 3.2.57 of this macOS host it is. On a bash 5 it may not be; that was not tried here. The runner is POSIX only, and the script targets macOS bash 3.2. Timed with this command, in an environment with no `LANG` or `LC_*`, as the tests run it:

      import json, os, subprocess, tempfile, time

      SUBST = 'stripped="$(cat "$1")"; stripped="${stripped//[[:space:]]/}"; echo "${#stripped}"'
      TR = 'stripped="$(tr -d \'[:space:]\' <"$1")"; echo "${#stripped}"'
      env = {"PATH": os.environ["PATH"], "HOME": os.environ["HOME"]}  # as the tests run it: no LANG, no LC_*
      for rules in (100, 300):
          listing = [{"id": "Build", "permissions": [
              {"action": "read", "resource": "/some/path/%d" % i, "effect": "allow"} for i in range(rules)]}]
          with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile("w", suffix=".json", delete=False) as fh:
              json.dump(listing, fh, indent=2)
          for name, code in (("substitution", SUBST), ("tr", TR)):
              started = time.monotonic()
              try:
                  out = subprocess.run(["/bin/bash", "-c", code, "_", fh.name], env=env, capture_output=True,
                                       text=True, timeout=60).stdout.strip()
              except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
                  out = "no answer in 60 s"
              print("%6d bytes  %-12s %5.2f s  %s" % (os.path.getsize(fh.name), name, time.monotonic() - started, out))
          os.unlink(fh.name)

  Output:

          10646 bytes  substitution  4.96 s  6222
          10646 bytes  tr            0.01 s  6222
          32046 bytes  substitution 60.00 s  no answer in 60 s
          32046 bytes  tr            0.01 s  18822

  The live-size test's listing is 36932 bytes (measured with the test's own construction). The live listing was reported as about 30 KB; that figure was not re-measured. The substitution took about 5 s at 10646 bytes and had not answered after 60 s at 32046 bytes. The reported size is near the second point and the runner's limit is 30 s, but nothing was timed at the reported size or between those two points, and no curve was fitted to them.

### Run-summary mutants: same-side and equivalent rows, and the paired edges

The killer lists of the BISHOP rows name tests of `RunDecidesOnBishopCalls` only. Every class that runs the script on a stub result goes through the same summary, so a row can fail tests in other classes too, and those are not listed.

- **BISHOP-NOT-DONE-NEVER and BISHOP-NOT-DONE-INVERTED share the identical message on their read-completed-no-start tests.** The `read completed, no start` test of each kind fails with the same message under both rows: exit 0 with the same closing line. On a run where only triage_run_start is missing, "never report the start" and "report the start when it completed" both leave the start unreported, so the run passes under either row and the observable is the same. This is an inherent shared kill for that edge, not two independent kills. The rows differ on the other edges: a clean run with a completed start fails under BISHOP-NOT-DONE-INVERTED only, and a run with no completed start and no other missing call passes under both.
- **The text pair BISHOP-TEXT-TOOL-ERRORS and BISHOP-TEXT-NOT-DONE is same-side, not opposite edges.** Each edits the wording of one reason, on a different branch of the run summary. A wording edit has no opposite edge of its own. The Mirror column names the other row only because `check_mutants.py` accepts a mirror only when the row it names names it back. The opposite edges of those branches are recorded by BISHOP-ERR-IGNORED and BISHOP-ERR-ANY-TOOL for the tool-error reason, and by the BISHOP-NOT-DONE rows for the missing-call reason.
- **The order edges are BISHOP-ORDER-LATE-ERROR-FORGIVEN against BISHOP-RETRY-NEVER-FORGIVEN.** The ordering rule has two edges. A later completed call of a tool forgives an earlier error of it, and BISHOP-RETRY-NEVER-FORGIVEN, which forgives nothing, fails the tests that pin that. An earlier completed call does not forgive a later error, and the BISHOP-ORDER-LATE-ERROR-FORGIVEN rows, which forgive it, fail the tests that pin that. The Mirror column pairs each of them with a different row, because `check_mutants.py` accepts a mirror only when the row it names names it back: the LATE rows with the UNRESOLVED rows, which invert the polarity of the guard each LATE row edits, and BISHOP-RETRY-NEVER-FORGIVEN with BISHOP-RETRY-FORGIVEN-BY-ANY-TOOL. BISHOP-RETRY-NEVER-FORGIVEN is killed on exit status by the retry tests, and on reason text alone by the retried-then-errored-again tests: a mutant that forgives nothing leaves two errors of the write where the code leaves one, both exit 1, and only the count in the reason tells them apart.
- **BISHOP-ORDER-LATE-ERROR-FORGIVEN-AT-APPEND and BISHOP-ORDER-LATE-ERROR-FORGIVEN-AT-CHECK are equivalent in exit status and not in reason text.** Each forgives an error that arrives after a completed call of its tool. The first guards the append with `name not in completed`; the second subtracts the completed tools' errors after the loop. Both fail a run exactly when some bishop-triage tool has an error and no call of that tool completed anywhere in the run, so no input separates them by exit status. That is an argument from the code, backed by a bounded sweep and not proved for every input: the sweep ran every sequence of up to five bishop-triage tool_use events over two tools and two statuses, each after a completed start, read and finish, on the program of this change, and found none on which the two rows exit differently. It is a one-off run and no test repeats it. They differ in the reason. The second counts the unfiltered list, as the code does, so it names a late error of a tool that completed beside an unresolved error of another tool; the first never appended that late error and does not name it. `test_late_error_of_one_tool_beside_an_unresolved_error_of_another_names_both` separates them on that text: it kills the first row and not the second, so the two rows do not share every killer. They still share the others, and the same first failure on the late-error tests, which is an inherent shared kill and not two independent kills. They are two rows because the review named both as alternatives. Their opposite edges, BISHOP-ORDER-UNRESOLVED-ERROR-DROPPED-AT-APPEND and BISHOP-ORDER-UNRESOLVED-ERROR-DROPPED-AT-CHECK, stand in the same relation: each fails a run exactly when an error stands whose tool completed before it and no completed call of that tool follows it, and the same test kills the first and not the second. Both AT-CHECK rows keep the in-loop filter. For BISHOP-ORDER-LATE-ERROR-FORGIVEN-AT-CHECK the subtraction removes every error the filter removes, so the row matches dropping the filter and subtracting after the loop. For BISHOP-ORDER-UNRESOLVED-ERROR-DROPPED-AT-CHECK the filter is not subsumed: dropping it would keep the early errors of a completed tool, so that row is not the same as dropping the filter.
- **The parse and shape guards are compounds, so each has an edit per operand and one for the whole.** `elif steps == 0 and unparsed:` has BISHOP-PARSE-REASON-MISSING for the whole guard, BISHOP-PARSE-REASON-ON-NO-STEPS-RUN for the `unparsed` operand dropped, so a run with no steps and every line parsed gets the parse reason, and BISHOP-PARSE-REASON-ON-STEPPED-RUN for the `steps == 0` operand dropped, so a stray or truncated line fails a run whose calls all completed. BISHOP-PARSE-REASON-STEPS-INVERTED is the opposite edge of the last. `if name and status:` has BISHOP-SHAPE-NEVER-COUNTED for the whole guard, BISHOP-SHAPE-STATUS-NOT-REQUIRED for the status operand dropped and BISHOP-SHAPE-NAME-NOT-REQUIRED for the name operand dropped, with BISHOP-SHAPE-NAMELESS-ONLY as the opposite edge of the name row. Each operand row has its own test, so the two do not share a kill: `test_tool_call_without_a_status_gives_the_shape_reason` kills BISHOP-SHAPE-STATUS-NOT-REQUIRED and not BISHOP-SHAPE-NAME-NOT-REQUIRED, and `test_tool_call_without_a_name_gives_the_shape_reason` kills the second and not the first, each with its own label in the first failure line. The mirrors of those rows are killed by the clean runs instead.
- **Shape drift is judged on the run itself.** Current policy: drift on any field, cost included, fails the run even when every call completed, and no mode logs drift without failing. A field the summary checks, when it is not in the shape the summary reads, is recorded by `read`, and a line that is JSON but not an object by its own guard. Either fails the run with the field named, and a run that has one is not also named for a missing call, because the event that was read as empty may be the call. A line that is not JSON is judged otherwise: it counts toward `unparsed`, which only a run with no steps is judged on, because a stray line cannot hide a call from the parser. Every site that goes through `read` is tested on each class of value. Null or absent reads as empty and is not drift, except for a whole line. A value of the wrong type is drift whether it is falsy or truthy: a `0`, `""`, `[]` or `false` where an object is read is drift, where the `or {}` this replaced read it as empty, and a string site and a number site are held to the same rule with the values that are not their type. A bool is not a number, so a cost of `false` or `true` is drift. An empty value of the right type is not drift (a cost of 0, an empty text, an empty object), and a test pins that too. Every field the loop reads goes through `read`, with exceptions, which are not checked: a step's `reason` and a text event's `messageID` are printed or compared and never decide the exit status or the reason, so a wrong-typed one changes only the `stop=` and the closing words shown. The message of an error event is chosen from the message in its data, its message and its type. Each goes through `read` before the first with text is taken, so a wrong-typed one is drift even when it is falsy and even when an earlier one is used. `tool` and `status` are read too, so a finish call whose status is `5`, or whose tool is a list, is drift with its field named and not a missing triage_run_finish. A cost that is a number is added as it is: an infinity or NaN, which the parser reads as numbers, passes (observed by hand, not tested), and only an integer too large for a float stops the summary, which the handler below names. The rows: the guards in `read` have a row for each value class. BISHOP-DRIFT-READ-NEVER-RECORDS and BISHOP-DRIFT-READ-NULL-RECORDED are the two edges for null against the rest. BISHOP-DRIFT-READ-TRUTHY-ONLY records only a truthy wrong-typed value, so a falsy one reads as empty, and BISHOP-DRIFT-READ-FALSY-ONLY records only a falsy one; those are the falsy and truthy classes. The type check has BISHOP-DRIFT-READ-BOOL-AS-NUMBER, which matches with `isinstance` so a bool passes, and BISHOP-DRIFT-READ-FALSY-REJECTED, which takes only a truthy value of the right type. Each call of `read` has rows named BISHOP-DRIFT-<FIELD>-UNREAD and BISHOP-DRIFT-<FIELD>-ALWAYS. The first returns the call to a raw read and the second makes the call record every value. Each site has one test of falsy wrong-typed values and one of truthy, a subtest per value, and an UNREAD row of that site kills both. The null and absent class and the right-typed falsy class are tested for all sites together, by the tests whose names begin `test_null_and_absent_` and `test_right_typed_falsy_`, each with a variant for error events. Each good-value test, which is the clean run or one of those controls, is killed by an ALWAYS row.
- **The reason of an error event is the first of its values that has text, and the fallback is `error`.** BISHOP-ERRMSG-PICK-FIRST takes the first value whether it is empty or not, and BISHOP-ERRMSG-PICK-NONE takes none; they are the two edges, and an empty message with text after it is what separates them from the code. BISHOP-ERRMSG-FALLBACK-EMPTY and BISHOP-ERRMSG-FALLBACK-WORDED each change the word given when no value has text. They are same-side, not opposite edges: a fallback has no opposite edge of its own, and the Mirror column names the other row only because `check_mutants.py` accepts a mirror only when the row it names names it back. Both are killed by the error events that carry no message.
- **A finish that closed the run as failed is judged, and the line says so.** A triage_run_finish that did not end in error and says `failed` in its input marks the run, and the ERROR line then begins `ERROR run closed as failed`. The condition has an operand for each of the following, each with a row and its opposite: the call did not end in error (BISHOP-RUNFAILED-ERRORED-FINISH reads an errored finish as well, BISHOP-RUNFAILED-ERRORED-ONLY reads only an errored one), the call is a triage_run_finish (BISHOP-RUNFAILED-ANY-TOOL reads any call, BISHOP-RUNFAILED-NOT-FINISH reads every call but that one), and the status in its input is `failed` (BISHOP-RUNFAILED-NEVER-SET never marks, BISHOP-RUNFAILED-STATUS-ANY marks every finish). The run fails with or without the mark when the finish errored, so the errored-finish row is killed on the wording of the ERROR line and not on the exit status: `test_errored_finish_with_status_failed_is_a_tool_error_not_a_run_closed_as_failed` asserts the tool error is named and the mark is not. The mark is the only reason a run closed as failed fails, so `test_finish_closed_as_failed_fails_the_run_with_the_failed_flag` asserts that no reason is named after it. A finish that says `done` is not marked, which every clean run shows.
- **The summary program fails closed with the exception type named.** Its loop and its report sit inside `try` with `except Exception`, which prints `ERROR reason=summary stopped on <type>` and exits 3, so a result the program was not written for fails the run with a reason where an uncaught exception left an empty one. A guarded read for each case was the other option. It was not taken: each would name only the case it was written for, the cases are classes of exception with no common cause, and the handler also names the ones nobody has met. The cost is that a stop names the type and not the field. The cases the tests drive are a result file that is not UTF-8, a line nested too deeply to decode, an integer cost too large for a float, and a text the output cannot encode (a lone surrogate); each has its own test and its own exception name. The handler has an edit for each class: BISHOP-HANDLER-ONLY-<CLASS> catches only that class and BISHOP-HANDLER-NOT-<CLASS> catches every class the tests drive but that one, so each test is needed by one row and the two rows are complements. BISHOP-HANDLER-NEVER catches nothing a run raises and BISHOP-HANDLER-CATCHES-EXIT catches the exits of the program, which turns a clean run into a stop. BISHOP-HANDLER-NO-REPORT prints nothing and BISHOP-HANDLER-EXIT-ZERO exits 0 after printing, the two halves of failing closed with a name. BISHOP-HANDLER-TYPE-UNNAMED and BISHOP-HANDLER-TYPE-WITH-DETAIL are same-side, as the fallback rows are: both change what follows `stopped on`, and the test asserts the line to its end so a message after the name fails it. The file is opened as UTF-8 by name so the answer does not depend on the locale: BISHOP-OPEN-LATIN1 accepts every byte and BISHOP-OPEN-ASCII refuses valid UTF-8. The controls (a valid non-ASCII text, a line nested deeply but readable, a large cost a float holds) pass under the handler rows that only widen what is caught. The handler does not cover the claude engine branch above it, which has its own `try` and was left as it was. Rows of the handler that are not each other's mirror can share a first failure line, because two rows that leave the same class uncaught fail the same test first with the same message (BISHOP-HANDLER-NEVER and BISHOP-HANDLER-ONLY-ENCODE both leave a result that is not UTF-8 uncaught, for one). That is a shared kill on that class, and it is not independent coverage of it: what each row adds is the test its killer list names that the other does not, and every mirror pair differs in its first failure.
- **A blank line is a line that does not parse as JSON.** A result of blank lines and nothing else gets the parse reason, hedged with `format changed?`, where the no-steps reason would be exact. It is left as it is: the run fails either way, a blank line in a run with steps changes nothing because `unparsed` is read only when there are no steps, and skipping blank lines would add a guard, and a pair of rows, to change the wording of one reason.
- **`failed` does not test `steps == 0`.** The branches that build `problems` give every run with no steps a reason, so `bool(problems)` already fails it. The operand was removed, not kept, because no test can kill it: a mutant that restored it would change no outcome. The tests of those reasons are what pin a run with no steps.
- **The classify read has a widening row and its own-rejected mirror.** BISHOP-CLASSIFY-READ-WIDENED accepts process's read for classify, and BISHOP-CLASSIFY-READ-OWN-REJECTED accepts no read for classify, as the process and grade rows do. The decoy `RunDecidesOnBishopCalls.test_classify_read_of_another_kind_exits_1` is a killer of the widened row. The narrowing rows BISHOP-CLASSIFY-NO-RECLASSIFY-READ and BISHOP-CLASSIFY-NO-NEXT-READ are unchanged.

### Python subtests and the runner

`scripts/mutate.py` runs each Python killer as a `Class.method` selector. It cannot select a subtest, and `parse_python` keeps only the first failing block of each method, so a verdict line names one subtest. The unittest process itself runs every subtest, and each mutant's log holds a `FAIL:` block for each one that fails. The table below was generated from the logs of the full run (`make mutate ID=...` over every GUARD row), for the tests that have subtests; the first assertion is the last `AssertionError` line of each block, cut where it quotes the log. For the `LayeredConfig` and `HelpText` tests, which give each assertion its own message, that message follows a dash, and the temporary paths and ports are masked. The `ConfigProbeClassification` rows keep the whole first line of the assertion, cut at 110 characters, with the case name in it and the temporary directory masked as `<tmp>`; a message that follows the quoted reason is cut off with it. Reproduce it by running the same `make mutate` and reading `grep '^FAIL:'` in each mutant's log, in the log directory the run's first line names. A killer without subtests has one outcome and is not listed.

## Mutation testing

`scripts/mutate.py` runs the active mutants in [`mutants.json`](mutants.json).
For each mutant it refuses unless the file is clean against HEAD: `git status
--porcelain --ignored` for the file must print nothing. It then plants the edit
alone, runs the mutant's killers, and restores the file. The restore is verified
(`restore_and_verify` in the script holds the checks) before the file counts as
restored. Each killer's full output goes to a per-mutant log. The runner is POSIX
only and refuses elsewhere.

    make mutate                    # every active mutant
    make mutate ID='GO-KEY M2'     # selected ids only

A mutant is KILLED when at least one of its killers fails and every killer
reached a verdict. A killer that did not reach one is not a kill; the mutant is
INVALID, with the reason printed beside it. `mutate_one` and `run_killers` in
the script decide each case. A killer that passes is listed as not failing.
SHARED-TEXT is printed when a mutant and its mirror fail with the same message;
the run then fails, because a shared kill is not two kills.
The text compared is the first failing killer's, taken in the order the spec
lists the killers, so that order matters: re-sorting a `killers` list can turn
two distinct texts into one. `MUT-DIGITS2` and `MUT-DIGITS3` rely on it, as each
lists a different test first.

Each killer run is bounded by `--timeout SECONDS` (default 600). Python killers
run as one `unittest -v` process per mutant, with `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`
and `python3 -B -I`, so the timeout bounds that process. Go killers run the
parent test with `go test -v -run`, one process per selector, and each selector
picks the subtests it names. Logs go to a temporary directory unless
`--log-dir` is given. Before a file is planted, its entry is written to
`mutate-unrestored.json` in the git directory (`.git/` in a normal checkout), with the log directory and the saved original. The
entry is removed when that file's restore is verified. A refused run that finds
a dirty file names the saved original of the earlier run that left it planted,
when that copy still exists, so the file can be compared with its copy. The
marker is replaced atomically, so a kill cannot leave it half-written. A marker
that does not parse refuses the run before anything is planted; the message names
the file and the recovery step (`git checkout -- <file>` for any modified file,
then delete the marker).

One run at a time. A run holds an exclusive lock on `mutate.lock` in the git
directory, and a second run refuses. Two runs on one working tree would plant over
each other's files and read each other's mutants, so this is a correctness rule
and not only a guard for the marker. The operating system releases the lock when
the process ends, however it ends.

Exit status is listed under `--help` and here; `--help` prints `EXIT_DOC`. A test
in `scripts/test_mutate.py` fails when the rows of this table and `EXIT_DOC` differ
in either direction.

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| 0 | every selected mutant KILLED, every restore verified, tree unchanged, no SHARED-TEXT |
| 1 | a mutant SURVIVED or was INVALID, a restore failed, or the tree changed |
| 2 | refused before anything was planted; the message names the cause |
| 3 | a required tool (git, or go for a Go mutant) is not installed or cannot answer |
| 4 | every mutant KILLED, but a mutant and its mirror fail with the same message |
| 5 | interrupted by a signal or Ctrl-C; the planted file, if any, was restored and verified |

An interrupt by a signal in `HANDLED_SIGNALS` (`scripts/mutate.py`) stops the run.
Each killer runs in its own process group, and a timeout or an interrupt kills
that group; a process that leaves the group (`setsid`, a double fork) is not
reached. If a planted file is not restored and verified, the run prints
`RESTORE FAILED` with the path of the saved original and exits 1 instead of 5,
because the file may still hold the mutant. A restore that never ran counts as
not verified. A signal during a restore does not cut it short: it is retried or
recorded, and the run stops once the restore is verified.

Known limitation: signals are not blocked between a plant and its restore, so a
handled signal can land at a point the restore does not protect. Examples, not a
complete list. A signal in the runner's `finally` block before the restore call, or
in the handling of an earlier interrupt during the restore, leaves the file planted,
and the run reports `RESTORE FAILED` and exits 1. A signal after the runner marks
the plant and before the protected block begins is reported the same way, though
nothing was written, so that report is a false alarm. A signal that lands in a
killer's process-group start-up before its protected block is entered, or in its
cleanup before the group is killed, leaves that group running; the restore still
runs and is verified, and the run prints that every restore is verified and exits 5
without reporting the group.

Anything that ends the process without letting the runner's code run skips every
restore. Nothing in the runner can handle that; the next run refuses on the dirty
file and names the saved copy recorded in the git directory's
`mutate-unrestored.json`.

The runner and the record check are tooling, not product code. DIR-017 governs
the product invariants the mutants target, so the tooling is not given mirrored
mutants of its own. It is covered by the per-edge unit tests in
`scripts/test_mutate.py` and `scripts/test_check_mutants.py`, and by controls that
run it against deliberately corrupted inputs (DIR-001).

`make test` runs the record check, not the mutants. The check takes a fraction of
a second; a mutant run takes minutes.

## Layout values at the seam

The directory and file names the importer and the reconciler read are declared
once. The Go values are `profile.Bishop.Layout` in `internal/profile/profile.go`.
The Python values are `BISHOP_LAYOUT` in `scripts/reconcile-memory.py`.

Only the missions folder name has been checked, against the goldens and the
unit tests above. Changing it to `missionz` in each language fails the golden
and the lookup tests in that language (SEAM-GO and SEAM-PY above). No other
layout value is claimed as pinned; see "What the goldens cannot see" for the
values the goldens do not read.
